# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Five-year relative survival for pancreatic cancer is 13.7% in the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results registry [@SEER2026]. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), expression data can help identify molecular programs associated with survival. Section 1.3 of the literature review describes two limitations of the usual analysis of prognostic tumor and stromal programs. An unsupervised factorization identifies the programs before testing their associations with survival. A program that predicts survival but explains little expression variation can be missed, because cell-composition variation dominates an expression-only fit (Section 1.3.2). The Cox model also treats the estimated program scores as if they were measured without error. This can bias the coefficients, and second-step standard errors omit the uncertainty from estimating the scores (Section 1.3.3). DeSurv lets survival guide discovery, but it reports penalized point estimates and tunes its rank and supervision strength by cross-validation [@Young2026].

This chapter develops survival-supervised Bayesian matrix factorization (SSBMF), which jointly fits an empirical-Bayes factorization of expression and a Cox model. Each patient's risk score is a weighted sum of their expression projected onto the program loadings, so a new patient's risk is computed from their measurements alone. Because the loadings appear in both the factorization and the risk score, survival can in principle change which programs are found. A survival weight $w_S$ sets the weight of the Cox likelihood relative to the expression likelihood. Posterior inference for the survival coefficients accounts for uncertainty in the loadings.

The earlier SSBMF model set the survival contribution to the loading update to zero. A configuration that included survival in that update was evaluated in a pre-registered October 15 check. Its mean difference in external concordance against the earlier model was $\Delta C=-0.003$ (95% CI $-0.029$ to $0.024$). The interval crossed the registered margin of $-0.02$, so the check did not establish noninferiority or a gain in concordance.

We derived and checked the variational algorithm, then used simulations to examine recovery of a low-variance prognostic program, false activity, calibration and convergence. In two PDAC training cohorts we used cross-validation to compare survival weights and feature sets. We evaluated the fixed model in five external series against rank-matched empirical Bayes matrix factorization (EBMF) followed by Cox regression. External concordance was similar, and calibration slopes were closer to one in four of the five series. DeSurv and an elastic-net Cox model trained on the same patients performed similarly. At $w_S=1$ the supervised and unsupervised loadings correlated 1.000, so the differences come from the joint coefficient update. In simulations with a very low-variance planted program, survival improved recovery.

We next aim to choose a supervision strength that improves program recovery when the signal supports it, to extend the model to expression and DNA methylation with separate loading priors, and to select rank from the data.

# Methods

## Model {#sec-model}

For $n$ patients and $p$ genes, let $Y$ ($n\times p$) hold log-scale expression standardized within each cohort. The expression model is
$$
Y = LF^\top + E,\qquad E_{ij}\sim N(0,\tau_j^{-1}),
$$
where $L$ ($n\times K$) holds patient scores on $K$ programs, $F$ ($p\times K$) holds gene loadings, and $\tau_j$ is the noise precision of gene $j$. Survival follows a Cox proportional hazards model [@Cox1972; @Cox1975] with Breslow handling of ties [@Breslow1974] and linear predictor
$$
\eta_i=\sum_{k=1}^K z_{ik}\beta_k,\qquad Z = YF .
$$
Here $z_{ik}$ is patient $i$'s expression projected onto program $k$'s loadings, and $\beta_k$ is the log hazard ratio per unit of that score. We call this the YFB parameterization, after $\eta=(YF)\beta$. The alternative, $\eta=L\beta$, puts the latent scores in the Cox model, so a new patient's risk needs their scores to be estimated first. A comparison of the two is proposed work (@sec-comparators).

Every entry of $L$ and of $F$ has a point-Laplace prior, a mixture of a point mass at zero and a Laplace distribution, with its mixing proportion and scale estimated by empirical Bayes for each program [@Willwerscheid2025]. The prior lets a loading be exactly zero and lets a whole program shrink to zero. Each coefficient has a Normal prior $\beta_k\sim N(0,\sigma_k^2)$ with $\sigma_k^2$ estimated. $Z$ has no prior of its own: it is a fixed function of the observed $Y$ and the loadings, so its posterior moments follow from those of $F$. The objective combines the expression likelihood and the Cox partial likelihood conditional on $Y$.

## Survival weight and objective {#sec-weight}

The model is fitted by maximizing an evidence lower bound (ELBO) over a factorized posterior $q=\prod_k q(l_k)\,q(f_k)\,q(\beta_k)$, the priors and $\tau$:
$$
\mathcal F = E_q\log p(Y\mid L,F,\tau) + w_S\,E_q\,\ell_{\mathrm{Cox}}(YF\beta) - \sum_k\left[\mathrm{KL}(q_{l_k}\Vert g_{l_k}) + \mathrm{KL}(q_{f_k}\Vert g_{f_k}) + \mathrm{KL}(q_{\beta_k}\Vert g_{\beta_k})\right].
$$
The survival term has unit weight at $w_S=1$. More generally the objective is a variational bound for an update that raises the Cox partial likelihood to the power $w_S$ [@Bissiri2016; @HolmesWalker2017]. The same $w_S$ enters every update that involves survival and the monitored objective.

Rescaling a program's scores, loadings and coefficient together leaves the likelihood unchanged. After each sweep, each nonzero program is rescaled so that its posterior mean projection $Y E[f_k]$ has standard deviation 1 in the training data. This fixes the units of $\beta_k$ (log hazard ratio per standard deviation of the program score) and makes one value of $w_S$ mean the same thing for every program. At $w_S=0$ survival drops out of every update, including that of $\beta$, so the fitted coefficients are zero. The unsupervised comparator is built from that fit: we take its loadings and fit a separate Cox model to the training scores $Y E[F]$. We call this the two-step fit. Both arms use the same rank and preprocessing. The comparison captures the combined effect of including survival in the loading update and estimating the Cox coefficients jointly under a Normal shrinkage prior.

Survival enters the factorization through the loading update. The Cox term contributes to both the precision and the linear term of that update. We use the fraction of loading precision due to the Cox term, called the survival share, to compare the relative information in the two likelihoods. The derivation shows that it grows with $w_S$, with the squared coefficient and with the number of events, and falls roughly as $1/p^2$ for a program of fixed variance share and as the square of that variance share. Survival therefore has the most influence on low-variance programs, which are the ones supervision is meant to find, and almost none on dominant programs.

## Variational inference {#sec-vi}

The Cox partial log-likelihood is not conjugate to any prior. At each sweep it is replaced by a second-order expansion around the current linear predictor, keeping the diagonal of the Hessian, so that each update has the form of a normal-means problem solved with the ebnm package [@Willwerscheid2025]. Taking expectations under $q$, the expansion contributes the variance of $\eta_i$ as well as its mean. The coefficient update uses the posterior second moment of each score, $E[z_{ik}^2]=\bar z_{ik}^2+\sum_j y_{ij}^2\operatorname{Var}(f_{jk})$, rather than its plug-in square. The second term propagates loading uncertainty into the variational coefficient update. The loading update has an expression part and a survival part. The survival part adds $w_S$ times the Cox curvature to each loading's precision, and genes are updated one at a time so that each sees the scores refreshed by the genes before it.

One sweep updates the Taylor expansion, then for each program the coefficient, the scores $l_k$ and the loadings $f_k$, then the noise precisions, and then rescales the programs. Scores and loadings start from a truncated singular value decomposition. Fitting stops when the relative change in the ELBO falls below $10^{-5}$, or after 300 sweeps. The full derivation, the update schedule and a one-page algorithm are in the project derivation document. A separate script checks each update against a brute-force evaluation of the expected objective and against the code (73 checks).

A nonempty program is called survival-active when its coefficient has positive posterior SD and $|E\beta_k|/\mathrm{SD}(\beta_k)\ge1.96$. In simulation, recovery requires an absolute loading correlation of at least 0.7, an active coefficient and the correct coefficient sign after aligning the loadings. A survival-active program that matches no planted prognostic program counts as false-active. A count of false-active programs does not say how much they affect the risk score. We therefore also report their share of the variance of the risk score and their standardized coefficients.

## Choosing the survival weight {#sec-choose-weight}

The real-data comparison uses $w_S=1$, which performed best in the first simulation study and was retained after five-fold cross-validation on the PDAC training data (@sec-res-cv). That choice keeps the coefficient update at its Bayesian weight, but it leaves the survival share on real data very small (@sec-res-cv). A larger fixed weight is not a solution, since fixed weights of 40 or more did not converge with 2,000 genes in simulation (@sec-res-sim).

We have tested one way of setting the weight from the data. In a variant of the objective, $w_S$ multiplies both the Cox term and $\mathrm{KL}(q_\beta\Vert g_\beta)$. The coefficient update is then the same as at $w_S=1$, and only the loadings see survival at weight $w_S$. The weight is chosen for each dataset from $\{1,2,5,10,20,50\}$ by five-fold cross-validated partial log-likelihood [@Verweij1993], with ties going to the smaller weight. A second variant replaces the factorized posterior for $\beta$ with a joint Gaussian. Both were evaluated in simulation (@sec-res-sim). The same rule was registered for the PDAC training data, with nested cross-validation to estimate the concordance of the whole procedure (@sec-res-cv).

We will compare this rule with two alternatives for choosing the weight. The first calibrates the power on the partial likelihood. SafeBayes chooses the power that minimizes a sequential predictive loss [@Grunwald2017], and Holmes and Walker match the expected information in the power posterior to that of a correctly specified model [@HolmesWalker2017]. The second divides each loss by a normalizing constant and mixes them with one parameter, as DeSurv does for its reconstruction and Cox losses [@Young2026]. Expressed in the units of our objective, this rule sets the relative survival weight and also rescales the KL terms. Each candidate will be judged on the simulation grid of @sec-sim-design and on training cross-validation, with criteria registered before any fit. A candidate must recover planted programs at least as often as the matched two-step fit, with a mean of at most one false-active program per evaluation cell. The protocol will also register a bound on the risk-score contribution from nonmatched programs. The median calibration slope must lie between 0.8 and 1.25 in at least two of three variance cells, and at least 9 of 10 fits must converge in each cell. On the real data, it must not lower cross-validated concordance by more than one standard error relative to $w_S=1$. The recovery, false-activity, calibration and convergence criteria follow the completed simulations. The contribution criterion is proposed.

## Prediction in new cohorts {#sec-prediction}

The November comparison fixed the survival weight, feature-set arm and survival-screen arm from training data. The D4 preprocessing recipe and rank came from earlier analyses that used external concordance. Validation cohorts are log-transformed once where needed, standardized within their own cohort and restricted to the training genes. Genes missing from a cohort are left out of the projection. The risk score is $\eta = Y_{\text{new}}E[F]E[\beta]$ with the loadings and coefficients frozen at their training values, and its direction is fixed by the training fit before any validation outcome is seen.

## Simulation studies {#sec-sim-design}

Three simulation studies were registered before they were run (Table \ref{tab:sim-design}). All use the same generator: three true programs, the third of which is prognostic and carries a small, set share of the expression variance, with Weibull survival times and about 30% censoring. Every fit starts from rank seven. The first study (S-9) asks whether the survival-weighted fit recovers the planted program at 50 and 2,000 genes across a wide grid of fixed weights. The second (S-13) chooses the weight by cross-validation and compares the result with the matched two-step fit, and also runs permuted-survival null datasets. The third (S-14) lowers the planted share toward the detection threshold, where an unsupervised factorization starts to miss the program, and compares strong survival with a weaker, realistic survival signal.

## PDAC data and evaluation {#sec-data}

The model is trained on TCGA-PAAD (144 patients) and CPTAC (129) [@Raphael2017; @Cao2021], with 139 deaths among the 273 patients. The five held-out cohorts contain 616 records from 568 donors. They are Dijk [@Dijk2020], Moffitt GEO array [@Moffitt2015], PACA-AU array and PACA-AU RNA-seq [@Bailey2016], and Puleo array [@Puleo2018]. Every RNA-seq cohort is log-transformed once. Expression is standardized within each cohort. The D4 procedure ranks genes by their expression mean and variance in each training cohort and intersects the top 3,000 per cohort, leaving 2,218 genes [@Young2026]. No survival screen is applied. The rank is fixed at $K=7$, the rank of the earlier benchmark.

The configuration was chosen by five-fold cross-validation on the training patients, stratified by cohort and event status. This covered the survival weight, the number of genes (from 2,218 to all 17,900 shared genes) and the effect of applying a survival screen inside each fold. After that the fixed model was scored once in each validation cohort, and nothing was chosen from the validation results. External discrimination is Harrell's concordance [@Harrell1982] with percentile bootstrap intervals [@EfronTibshirani1993]. Differences between the supervised and two-step fits use a paired bootstrap within each cohort (2,000 replicates), pooled across cohorts by equally weighting the series-specific differences. A donor bootstrap keeps records from the same donor together while preserving the within-series concordance comparisons. Calibration is the slope of a Cox model of validation survival on the risk score, so a slope of 1 means the training coefficients have the right size. The PACA-AU array and RNA-seq series share 47 donors, and the RNA-seq series contains a repeated donor. We also report the pooled difference after excluding that series.

## Proposed extension to several data types {#sec-mmodal}

The single-modality model is the case $M=1$ of a model for $M$ matched data types with shared patient scores and modality-specific loadings:
$$
Y_m = LF_m^\top + E_m,\qquad E_{m,ij}\sim N(0,\tau_{mj}^{-1}),\qquad \eta_i=\sum_k z_{ik}\beta_k,\qquad Z=\sum_{m=1}^M Y_mF_m .
$$
Each program has a separate point-Laplace prior $g_{F_{mk}}$ for each modality. Estimating the priors by empirical Bayes allows a sparser prior for the much larger set of methylation sites. Every update keeps the single-modality form. The score update sums the expression terms over modalities, each $F_m$ update uses the joint score, and the coefficient update uses the joint score with its variance summed over modalities. With $M=1$ every formula reduces to the one above.

The derivation identifies a balance problem the single-modality model does not have. The precision of the shared scores sums over all features, so the modality with more features, methylation in the planned application, would dominate $L$, and the survival share falls with the total number of features. Modality-specific weights on the reconstruction terms may therefore be needed. They will be derived and checked in simulation before any real-data fit. We will implement the model in one fitter and check that its $M=1$ case reproduces the single-modality fit to numerical tolerance. We will evaluate the extension in two-modality simulations with modality-specific programs and one shared prognostic program. The planned application uses matched TCGA expression and methylation with validation in ICGC PACA-AU. We will test whether adding methylation improves external concordance over an expression-only fit. The criterion is a positive paired difference with an interval that excludes zero. We will also assess whether adding methylation identifies a prognostic program missed by the expression-only fit.

## Proposed rank selection {#sec-rank}

The working fit uses $K=7$ without pruning. In a simulation run after correcting the treatment of a flat coefficient likelihood, unpruned fits recovered the planted program in 17 of 20 and 19 of 20 datasets across the two noise levels. Ordinary and protected ELBO pruning each recovered 2 of 20 at both levels and retained median ranks of two and one. Both failed the registered recovery and rank criteria. We will evaluate rank selection under the supervised objective with replicated training cross-validation and assess whether the final rank varies by at most one across starting ranks while retaining planted prognostic programs.

## Comparators, risk groups and program classification {#sec-comparators}

Every comparator was trained on the same 273 training patients, and each score's direction was fixed on the training data. DeSurv used the authors' software, preprocessing and published settings (rank 3), which the authors selected on the same two training cohorts [@Young2026]. An elastic-net Cox model on the D4 genes [@Simon2011] chose its mixing and penalty parameters by cross-validation on the training folds. PurIST [@Rashid2020] entered as a Cox model on its basal-like probability. A clinical model was planned, but no stage, grade, age or margin field is recorded in both training cohorts and all five validation series, so it was not fitted. Unsupervised EBMF at ranks 7, 15 and 40 followed by Cox regression tested whether a larger unsupervised rank would close any gap. Pooled hazard ratios are per SD of each score from Cox models stratified by series, with robust intervals clustered on donor.

For risk groups, one cutpoint per score maximized the log-rank statistic on the out-of-fold training scores, with at least 20% of patients in each group, and was applied unchanged in every validation series. A program was called a main prognostic program when its standardized coefficient was at least 0.25 of the largest, its signed share of the risk-score variance, $\mathrm{Cov}(\eta_k,\eta)/\mathrm{Var}(\eta)$, was at least 5%, and it was survival-active in at least four of the five training folds after matching loadings with absolute correlation at least 0.7. These rules were registered before they were applied. A registered comparison with the $\eta=L\beta$ parameterization, which estimates each new patient's scores by fold-in under the frozen priors, remains to be run.

# Results

## Survival weight in simulation {#sec-res-sim}

With 2,000 genes and $w_S=1$, the survival-weighted fit recovered the planted program in 10 of 10 datasets in each of the three variance cells, with a mean of 0.9, 0.1 and 0.0 false-active programs, and every fit converged (Figure \ref{fig:sim-s9}). Five-fold training cross-validation chose $w_S=1$ in 55 of 60 datasets. The other choices were the weight targeting a survival precision share of 0.2 in three datasets and $w_S=10$ in two. Every fit with $w_S\ge40$ stopped at 300 sweeps without converging, and recovery fell in most cells. With 50 genes, all fixed positive weights recovered the program, and false activity rose with weight. The share-targeted arm did not recover the program. The cause of non-convergence at large weights has not been found. In those fits the largest $|E\beta_k|$ ranged from 17 to 26. The SD of the true predictor ranged from 9 to 26.

At 2,000 genes, the fitted risks at $w_S=1$ were attenuated. The median validation calibration slope was 1.45, 2.16 and 3.23 across the three variance cells, against about 1 for the true predictor. A slope above 1 means that the fitted risks are shrunk toward zero. Validation concordance ranged from 0.94 to 0.99. The survival share of the planted program's loading precision explains part of this. At $w_S=1$ it fell from 0.79–1.00 with 50 genes to 0.01–0.20 with 2,000.

```{=latex}
\caption{Survival-weighted fit with 2,000 genes against the survival weight $w_S$ (S-9): recovery of the planted program, mean number of false-active programs, median exact-time validation calibration slope, converged fits, median survival share of matched loading precision and mean validation concordance. Curves are grouped by the planted program's share of expression variance. Ten datasets per cell.}\label{fig:sim-s9}
```

The matched two-step fit uses the $w_S=0$ loadings and also recovers the planted program in 10 of 10 datasets in every one of these cells (Table \ref{tab:strength}). The preregistered comparison used an earlier unsupervised fit on uncentered input, which recovered 0 or 1 of 10, so it confounded centering with supervision. The supervised fits at $w_S=1$ converged with few false-active programs.

When the weight was chosen for each dataset by cross-validated partial log-likelihood (Figure \ref{fig:sim-s13}), the chosen weight grew with the strength of the planted program: 1 or 2 in the weakest cells, 5 at 1% variance and 10 at 5%. The rule never chose 20 or 50, the weights at which fits stopped converging. At the chosen weight, recovery equalled the two-step fit's in every cell. Validation concordance was equal in the two stronger cells and higher by 0.003 to 0.007 in the two weakest, and false activity was lower than the two-step fit's in the stronger cells. The coefficients stayed attenuated, with median slopes of 1.24 to 1.45 in the three strong-survival cells, compared with 0.96 to 1.16 for two-step. Neither variant met every registered criterion. Both failed the calibration band, and the block-weight variant had a null false-active rate of 1.1 at its most often chosen weight against a limit of 1. The joint posterior for $\beta$ gave the same recoveries and concordance as the factorized one, to within 0.004.

Supervision changed discovery only near the detection threshold (Figure \ref{fig:sim-s14}). With strong survival and a planted share of 0.05% of the expression variance, the supervised fit at $w_S=1$ recovered the program in 5 of 10 datasets. The two-step fit recovered none. Mean validation concordance was 0.156 higher in the supervised fit. The supervised fit had the higher concordance in 29 of the 30 strong-survival datasets, and the gain shrank as the program became easier to find, to 0.041 at a share of 0.1% and 0.008 at 0.2%. The registered recovery criterion still failed, because both fits averaged more than two false-active programs in the hardest cell. With realistic survival, where the true predictor gives a validation concordance of about 0.74, the gains were small: 0.038 at a share of 0.05%, where no fit recovered the program, and 0.002 to 0.008 at the larger shares. A fixed $w_S=5$ recovered the planted program in more datasets with strong survival and fewer datasets with realistic survival. Its calibration slopes ranged from 0.04 to 0.65. This contrast motivates choosing the weight from the data.

Points show individual datasets and diamonds show cell means for the paired differences. Ten datasets per cell.}\label{fig:sim-s14}
```{=latex}
\end{figure}
```

We also examined the combined contribution of the nonmatched programs, including those below the activity threshold. In the S-14 cells with planted shares of 0.1% and 0.2%, the median ratio of nonmatched to total risk-score variance reached 1.3% at $w_S=1$. Removing the nonmatched programs changed mean concordance by at most 0.008 across the supervised and two-step arms in these cells. At 0.05% planted share the median ratios ranged from 8.7% to 68.8%. With strong survival they were 8.7% for the supervised fit and 68.8% for two-step. These post hoc comparisons describe predictive contributions, separate from the registered count of false-active programs. In a simulation that planted one strong and one near-threshold prognostic program together, the supervised fit at $w_S=1$ and the two-step fit each recovered the near-threshold program in 9 of 10 datasets, while a fixed $w_S=5$ recovered it in 2.

The planned evaluation will compare the calibrated alternatives in @sec-choose-weight on the same grid and add cells with more realistic survival effects.

## Training cross-validation on PDAC {#sec-res-cv}

On the PDAC training data the supervised fit had a cross-validated concordance of 0.663 (SE 0.024), against 0.652 (SE 0.026) for the two-step fit, a paired difference of 0.011 (SE 0.005) (Table \ref{tab:training-cv}). Three programs were survival-active in the all-patient fit. Two of the five supervised fold fits stopped at the 300-sweep limit with the ELBO still changing by more than $10^{-5}$, but with small coefficients (largest $|E\beta|$ 0.46) and no sign of the instability seen at large weights in simulation.

```{=latex}
\begin{table}[!htb]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Fit & \shortstack{Mean fold $C$\\(SE)} & \shortstack{Pooled\\out-of-fold $C$} & \shortstack{CV partial\\log-likelihood} & \shortstack{Folds\\converged} & \shortstack{Survival-active\\programs} \\
\midrule
$w_S = 1$ & 0.663 (0.024) & 0.663 & $-$775.2 & 3/5 & 3 \\
Two-step & 0.652 (0.026) & 0.647 & $-$777.1 & 3/5 & 4 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{Paired fold difference ($w_S = 1$ minus two-step) \quad $+$0.011 (SE 0.005)} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Five-fold training cross-validation on the 2,218 selected genes (273 patients, 139 events). Convergence refers to the factorization in each arm. Activity is measured in the fit to all training patients using $|E[\beta_k]| \geq 1.96$ posterior SD for $w_S = 1$ and the Wald test for the two-step fit.}
\label{tab:training-cv}
\end{table}
```

Survival did not change the loadings. Its share of the loading precision was $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-6}$, against 0.01 to 0.2 in the 2,000-gene simulation, and the supervised and unsupervised loadings agreed at $|r|=1.000$ for every program. Two features of the real data combine to make the share this small. The real coefficients are small, at most 0.6 per standard deviation of the score, and the share scales with $E[\beta_k^2]$. The real programs are also high-variance programs with a large expression precision, whereas the simulated program carried 0.25% to 5% of the variance. The concordance difference therefore reflects the joint coefficient update with its Normal shrinkage prior.

The 2,218-gene set was preferred by the registered rule (Figure \ref{fig:size-curve}). Supervised concordance fell from 0.663 at 2,218 genes to between 0.643 and 0.648 at 8,000 genes and above, while the two-step fit stayed between 0.650 and 0.653, so the supervised fit's advantage reversed above 5,000 genes. All sizes were within one standard error of one another. By cross-validated partial log-likelihood the ordering differed slightly, so larger sets are not worse by every measure. Screening genes for a univariate survival association inside each fold gave gains of 0.003 to 0.012 over an outcome-free set of the same size, each within about one paired standard error, and no screened set beat the full 2,218-gene fit. On permuted-survival datasets the fit at $w_S=1$ produced 0.1 to 0.5 false-active programs per cell, within the registered limit of one.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/sup_real_size_curve.pdf}
\caption{Five-fold cross-validated concordance on the PDAC training cohorts (mean $\pm$ 1 SE over folds) against the number of genes, for the supervised fit ($w_S=1$) and the two-step fit.}\label{fig:size-curve}
\end{figure}
```

A refit that chose the weight by training cross-validated partial log-likelihood on these patients, over weights from 1 to 50, selected $w_S=1$. The curve was flat. The criterion changed from $-775.168$ at weight one to $-775.429$ at weight 50. Nested cross-validation gave $C=0.656$ (SE 0.027), compared with 0.663 at the fixed weight. At weight 50, survival supplied a median of $7.3\times10^{-5}$ of the loading precision for active programs, and the loadings still agreed with those of the unsupervised fit to the reported precision. The registered rule retained the existing fit and its external evaluation.

## External validation {#sec-res-external}

In the five held-out cohorts the supervised fit's concordance was 0.584 in Dijk, 0.537 in Moffitt, 0.656 in PACA-AU array, 0.681 in PACA-AU RNA-seq and 0.644 in Puleo, a mean of 0.620 (Table \ref{tab:external}, Figure \ref{fig:external}). It was equal to or higher than the two-step fit in every cohort. The equal-weight pooled difference was 0.007 (95% record-bootstrap CI $-0.002$ to $0.017$, donor-bootstrap CI $-0.003$ to $0.017$). Excluding PACA-AU RNA-seq gave 0.006 ($-0.003$ to $0.016$). Each interval includes zero. A Cox model stratified by cohort gave a hazard ratio of 1.37 (1.24 to 1.51) per standard deviation of the supervised risk score, and 1.35 (1.22 to 1.49) for the two-step score. With robust intervals clustered on donor these become 1.22 to 1.53 and 1.21 to 1.51. DeSurv refitted on the same training patients gave 1.43 (1.25 to 1.64), against 1.50 (1.31 to 1.72) in its publication [@Young2026].

## Comparison with other prognostic models {#sec-res-comparators}

The supervised fit's validation concordance was within noise of DeSurv and of the elastic-net Cox model trained on the same patients (Table \ref{tab:comparators}). The mean concordance over the five series was 0.620 for the supervised fit, 0.614 for DeSurv and 0.619 for elastic-net Cox. The paired differences were 0.007 ($-0.017$ to 0.030) against DeSurv and 0.001 ($-0.015$ to 0.018) against elastic-net Cox. The intervals against DeSurv, elastic-net Cox, PurIST and the two-step fit included zero. The elastic-net model selected the ridge penalty. PurIST alone had a mean concordance of 0.599. EBMF followed by Cox regression did worse at ranks 15 and 40 than at rank 7, with calibration slopes of 0.10 to 0.49 that show the unpenalized Cox step overfitting with 139 training deaths.

The training cutpoint was $-0.046$ SD for the supervised score and 0.526 SD for the two-step score. Applied unchanged in the validation series, it gave pooled high-versus-low hazard ratios of 1.52 (1.24 to 1.87) and 1.69 (1.32 to 2.16). The two estimates are not comparable, because the supervised cutpoint placed 297 of 616 validation records in the high-risk group and the two-step cutpoint placed 144. A smaller and more extreme high-risk group gives a larger hazard ratio when two scores rank patients equally well. In every series the supervised high-risk group held a larger proportion of Basal-like tumours by PurIST and of permissive CAF (permCAF) tumours by DeCAF. The supervised score's pooled hazard ratio per training SD was 1.51 unadjusted, 1.48 after adjusting for PurIST subtype and 1.40 after adjusting for DeCAF subtype.

## Programs {#sec-res-programs}

Three fitted programs were survival-active. Program 2 was protective at its positive pole ($E[\beta]=-0.405$), while the positive poles of Programs 3 and 5 were adverse (0.218 and 0.230). Table \ref{tab:programs} gives the coefficient estimates and the genes at both poles. Programs 2 and 3 met the registered classification rule (Table \ref{tab:program-rule}). Program 5 met the coefficient and variance thresholds but was survival-active in only three of the five training folds. Survival supplied at most $2.1\times10^{-6}$ of any program's loading precision, so no program is survival-dominated. In saved simulation fits the coefficient and variance parts of the rule kept the planted program in all 80 S-13 fits and rejected 35 of 36 false-active directions, but rejected only 61 of 128 in the two-step S-14 fits. At the protective pole of Program 2, the largest loadings included genes associated with exocrine and classical epithelial expression. Its adverse pole included \textit{LDHA}, \textit{PGK1} and \textit{SLC16A3}, consistent with the hypoxia and glycolysis enrichment in the full gene-set results. Program 3's adverse pole included ribosomal and proliferation-associated genes, with classical epithelial genes at the other pole. Program 5 showed mitotic and stromal or immune signatures, with a less specific subtype interpretation. Two of Program 3’s enriched Reactome sets are named for influenza and share leading ribosomal genes (Table \ref{tab:enrichment}).

The loadings matched the $w_S=0$ fit across all 2,218 genes (Figure \ref{fig:program-correspondence}). Across the 1,985 genes shared with the historical $\alpha_F=0$ fit, Program 2 matched historical Program 7 at $|r|=0.623$ and Program 3 matched historical Program 3 at $|r|=0.649$. Both pairs had opposite loading signs. The matched poles shared nine and three of their top 25 genes, respectively. Program 5's best historical match had $|r|=0.180$.

Separate external Cox regressions estimated protective associations for Program 2 in all five series. The estimates were adverse for Program 3 in four series and for Program 5 in two (Table \ref{tab:external-program-direction}). These regressions are unadjusted, so their directions need not agree with the coefficients from the joint training fit. The corresponding Kaplan--Meier curves (Figures \ref{fig:km-program-2} to \ref{fig:km-program-5}) group patients by the training coefficient's risk direction. Cohort-specific coefficient fits in TCGA-PAAD and CPTAC remain part of the planned evaluation.

Signature scores provide another comparison with published PDAC subtypes and stromal signatures. We averaged the available standardized genes in each published signature within each cohort and correlated those scores with fixed program scores. Program 2 correlated negatively with the Moffitt basal-like signature in pooled training data ($\rho=-0.71$) and across external series ($-0.78$ to $-0.71$). Program 3 correlated negatively with the Moffitt classical signature ($\rho=-0.76$ in training, $-0.84$ to $-0.57$ externally). Program 5's correlations with the DeSurv stromal-immune signature were weaker ($\rho=0.21$ in training, $-0.03$ to $0.23$ externally), so its enrichment gives limited evidence of a reproducible stromal association. Correlations with the saved PurIST basal-like probabilities agreed with the broad subtype directions. Across the external series, the correlations were $-0.64$ to $-0.45$ for Program 2, 0.30 to 0.79 for Program 3, and $-0.25$ to $-0.13$ for Program 5.

# Discussion

## Loading and coefficient estimates

The main change in the PDAC application was in the coefficient update. The joint fit propagates posterior loading uncertainty and shrinks the coefficients, and the slope comparison varies by series. The supervised and two-step loadings agreed to the reported precision. The observed differences therefore cannot establish improved molecular program discovery on these data.

The simulations show where supervised discovery can help and how far the current model gets there. A small survival weight acts mostly on low-variance programs, since the survival share grows as a program's variance share falls. Near the detection threshold the supervised fit found programs the two-step fit missed and predicted much better when survival was strong. When the planted program was easy to find, or survival was as weak as on the real data, the two fits were nearly the same. A larger fixed weight moved the loadings in strong-survival settings but overfit in realistic ones and failed to converge with 2,000 genes. Choosing the weight by cross-validated partial log-likelihood avoided those weights and adapted to the signal, but it left the coefficients attenuated in the strong-survival cells. That combination makes a data-driven weight the main open problem of the project.

A registered comparison with $\eta=L\beta$ will evaluate recovery and out-of-sample prediction together. In that model, a new patient's scores are estimated by fold-in under the frozen priors (@sec-comparators).

## Limitations

Historical analyses used the external panel to inform rank, preprocessing, the loading supervision weight $\alpha_F$, the number of frozen-loading sweeps and comparator configuration. No series in this panel is untouched. The donor bootstrap and the donor-clustered hazard-ratio intervals account for repeated donors while leaving the pooled estimand conditional on the observed series. DeSurv used its published settings rather than a new search on our training folds. Some training folds stopped at the sweep limit. The simulations use a single generator, and the strongest simulated survival signals exceed those observed in the real data.

## Continuing work

We will develop a data-driven survival weight that lets survival affect the loadings where the data support it. Candidates are the cross-validated weight already tested, a calibrated power on the partial likelihood, and normalized loss terms (@sec-choose-weight). Each will be judged against the registered simulation criteria and against training cross-validation on PDAC, and any configuration adopted on the training data will be scored once externally. The extension to several data types (@sec-mmodal) will start from a fitter that reproduces the current model for one modality. We will also assess rank selection under the supervised objective (@sec-rank). The remaining comparison (@sec-comparators) will place the method against the $L\beta$ parameterization.  We will release the selected model as an R package with a single fitting function and use it to regenerate the manuscript results.
